                    ### Question
                    A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a dog bite. The patient was intoxicated and pulled the dog’s tail while it was eating. The dog belongs to his friend and is back at his friend’s house currently. Physical exam is notable for a dog bite on the patient’s right arm. The wound is irrigated and explored with no retained bodies found. A tetanus vaccination is administered. Which of the following is appropriate management of this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Administer amoxicillin-clavulanic acid
opb. Administer the rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin
opc. Administer trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
opd. Close the wound with sutures and discharge the patient
ope. Discharge the patient with outpatient follow up

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In managing a dog bite, the primary concern is preventing infection, particularly from common pathogens like Pasteurella multocida. Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is effective against Pasteurella and is the recommended prophylactic antibiotic, aligning with consensus guidelines. The risk of rabies is low since the dog is known and can be observed, so rabies vaccination is not immediately necessary. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is not effective against Pasteurella and is not recommended. Suturing a dog bite wound is generally avoided to prevent trapping bacteria and increasing infection risk. After proper wound care and tetanus vaccination, discharging the patient with outpatient follow-up is appropriate if the wound is not high-risk. Therefore, administering amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is the most appropriate management step.
